🤿 Deep dive · Lesson 12 · 2 min read

Your AI Toolkit

How to ask AI good questions, check its answers, learn honestly with it, and keep growing your skills.

Asking well

What you get from a chatbot depends a lot on what you ask. A good prompt can have several ingredients. A role: “You are a friendly maths tutor.” Context: who you are and why you're asking. A clear task: exactly what you want. An example of the kind of answer you like. And a format: a list, a table, a short paragraph. You don't need all of them every time: a simple question can stay simple. If the answer isn't quite right, don't start over: reply and say what to change.

Checking answers

Remember lesson 9: a chatbot picks likely words, not checked facts. It can even invent sources that look real. So for anything that matters, check. Ask for sources, then open them: do they exist, and do they really say that? Compare the answer with a trusted website, a textbook or your teacher. Be extra careful when an answer sounds very sure but gives no evidence, when it has exact numbers, dates or quotes, or when it is about health, money or the news. A good habit: find important facts in at least two trusted places.

Did you know? Asking “Are you sure?” isn't a real check. A chatbot may just repeat its mistake, or politely swap a right answer for a wrong one. Check with a source instead.

Learning honestly with AI

AI can be a great tutor. It can explain something in a different way, give you a hint when you're stuck, quiz you before a test or comment on your own draft. Used as a ghostwriter that writes your work for you, it does the learning instead of you, and at many schools that's against the rules. Every school sets its own rules, so ask your teacher what is allowed, and say when AI helped you. And remember why homework exists: learning scientists have found that working things out yourself, even with mistakes along the way, helps you remember them better than reading a ready-made answer.

Did you know? A tutor prompt: “I'm stuck on this equation. Don't solve it for me: give me a hint for the next step, then check my answer.” You still do the thinking, and AI helps you get unstuck.

Your future with AI

AI is used in more and more fields. Doctors use it to help read scans, scientists to predict the shapes of proteins, farmers to spot sick plants, artists and game designers to try out ideas. Some tasks are already done by AI, and new kinds of work are appearing. The skills that matter most are very human: curiosity, maths and clear thinking, communication, and ethics, asking not only “Can we?” but also “Should we?” Knowing how AI works, as you now do, is a skill too. To keep learning, explore this site's AI Lab and try free online courses such as Elements of AI.

Did you know? In 2024, two Nobel Prizes went to work on AI. The physics prize went to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton, for discoveries that laid the foundations of machine learning with neural networks. Half of the chemistry prize went to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for AlphaFold, an AI that predicts the shapes of proteins.

Key points

  • A good prompt can have a role, context, a clear task, an example and a format.
  • Check what matters: open the sources, compare with trusted ones, and be careful when an answer sounds too sure.
  • Use AI as a tutor, not a ghostwriter: follow your school's rules and do the thinking yourself.

Check yourself

Your school allows AI for brainstorming, but not for writing your essay. Which is an honest way to use it?

  1. Ask AI for questions worth exploring, then research and write the essay yourself
  2. Let AI write the essay, then change a few words so it looks like yours
  3. Ask AI to write in a style that sounds like you, so nobody notices
Show the answer

Brainstorming questions with AI is what the rule allows, and the research and the writing, the thinking, stay yours. Changing a few words, or asking AI to copy your style, still means AI wrote the essay: it breaks the rule, and you miss the learning the essay was for.
